name: Zoe Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a marketing assistant at a pet food brand, dry food, treats, the lot. Half my day is writing product descriptions for online shops and the other half is planning promotions with the supermarkets, like which week the two-for-one on dog biscuits runs. I also fill in the forms the supermarkets want, which never end.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What keeps you going, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the supermarket side, seeing our display at the end of an aisle after weeks of emails. What wears me down is that I'm still slow at the numbers and my manager Paul double-checks everything I send. I use an AI tool now and then for the descriptions, mostly when I'm behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds like a fairly normal few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, that's that then. At work I'd say the tool is handy for first drafts and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I write descriptions for dog biscuits all day, and if AI just speeds that up, I'd spend the spare time arguing with supermarket buyers about shelf space. My job looks fine, and I've got about seven months saved plus my flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, use the tool a bit more for descriptions, and ask Paul to teach me the pricing spreadsheets. I'd keep overpaying the mortgage by a hundred a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I'd go home and walk the dog.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the flat. How did you manage it so young?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My nan left me some money, which covered the deposit on a small one-bedroom. The mortgage is about seven hundred a month, which is fine on my pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in this picture that would still bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paul checking everything. If I don't get quicker at the numbers, I'll be an assistant for years. That's on me, not AI.

say: I'd say **that's that** and move on.
I'd call the tool **handy for drafts** and leave it there.
think: I think faster **descriptions** just free me for supermarket work.
I'd feel secure with **seven months saved** and my own flat.
do: Use the AI tool **a bit more** for product descriptions.
Learn the **pricing spreadsheets** and keep overpaying the mortgage by a hundred.
feel: **Calm**, ready to go home and walk the dog.
S0.quote: I write descriptions for dog biscuits all day, and if AI just speeds that up, I'd spend the spare time arguing with supermarket buyers about shelf space.
fieldNote: Her flat came from her grandmother's **inheritance**, so her base feels solid.
Her real worry is her own **slowness with numbers**.
She treats the tool as **handy**, neither loving nor fearing it.

steps.text: Use the AI tool more often for online product descriptions
Ask her manager to teach her the pricing spreadsheets
Keep overpaying the mortgage by a hundred a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That feels close to what's actually starting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big shift but people will adjust, they always do. Online I'd probably not say much, maybe share an article.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the product descriptions are already half written by the tool, and I'm the half that's left. The supermarket forms and bookings are on the card too. If the marketing team shrinks, assistants are easy to cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the tools properly now that it's clear they work, maybe the course my company pays for. I'd put more into savings, two hundred extra a month, and keep the mortgage overpayments. I'd also start getting myself to the supermarket meetings in person, so the buyers know my face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd be fine for a while, but I can see the line coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you think meeting the buyers in person matters?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a buyer at a big supermarket can get a hundred perfect emails. What they remember is the person who turned up with samples and sorted the broken display.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who else on your team would feel this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leah, who does the social posts. She's lovely but her whole job is captions. I'd worry she goes before me.

say: I'd say it's a **big shift** but people adjust.
I'd **share an article** online rather than say much.
think: I think the tool already writes **half my descriptions**.
I'd see **assistants** as easy cuts if the team shrinks.
do: Take the company's **AI course** now that the tools are proven.
Save **two hundred** more a month and meet buyers **in person**.
feel: **Anxious**, fine for now but seeing the line coming.
S1.quote: The product descriptions are already half written by the tool, and I'm the half that's left.
fieldNote: She moves to the tools **once proven**, true to her steady nature.
She sees **face-to-face** buyer work as her protection.
She worries for her colleague **Leah** before herself.

steps.text: Take the company-paid course on AI marketing tools
Save an extra two hundred a month
Go to supermarket buyer meetings in person with samples

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's very quick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a huge change and we need a plan from government, not slogans. I'd say it at work too, which I don't usually do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my mortgage doesn't care whether my job went to a person or a machine; the payment still leaves on the first of the month. My desk work goes almost straight away. The only part that lasts a bit longer is lugging displays into stores, and robots come for that three years later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for a field sales job, the people who visit stores and set up the displays, because that's hands-on. I'd take a lodger in the spare corner, well, the sofa bed, for about four hundred a month. And I'd cut the extras, the takeaways and the holiday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd keep doing sums at midnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A lodger in a one-bedroom flat? That's quite a step.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is. My sister Megan might do it, actually, she's a vet nurse and always broke. Family is easier than a stranger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Paul, your manager?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask him straight whether my job exists next year. He's honest, he'd tell me.

say: I'd demand a **government plan**, not slogans.
I'd say it **at work** as well, which I rarely do about anything political.
think: I think my **mortgage** keeps going whether a person or machine took my job.
I'd see only the **display lugging** lasting, and robots take that three years later.
do: Apply for a **field sales** job setting up store displays.
Take a **lodger** for about four hundred and cut takeaways and holidays.
S2.quote: My mortgage doesn't care whether my job went to a person or a machine; the payment still leaves on the first of the month.
fieldNote: The **mortgage** makes the fast picture very concrete for her.
She spots the **hands-on** part of her job and moves toward it.
Family, her sister **Megan**, is her first thought for a lodger.

steps.text: Apply for a field sales job setting up store displays
Rent the sofa bed to her sister for about four hundred
Cut takeaways and cancel this year's holiday

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a bit more breathing space.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to plan if people start now. At work I'd suggest we talk about it at the team meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough to stop being the person who writes about pet food and become the person who gets it onto the shelf. That's the face-to-face, carry-the-boxes side, and it gets until about 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the AI tools fully for the descriptions now, to keep my numbers up. Within a year I'd ask to move into the field sales team. I'd keep saving the extra two hundred and overpay the mortgage harder, maybe three hundred a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steadier than the two-year one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the risk in that plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Field sales pays a bit less and there's a lot of driving. And if the supermarkets put robots on the shelves in 2034, I'm doing this again at 35.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you do it again at 35?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I suppose I'd have to. With the flat paid down more, it'd be less scary.

say: I'd say there's **time to plan** if people start now.
I'd suggest we raise it together at the next **team meeting**.
think: I think I can move to getting pet food **onto the shelf**.
I'd count on the **hands-on side** lasting until about 2034.
do: Use AI fully for **descriptions** to keep my numbers up.
Move into **field sales** and overpay the mortgage about **three hundred** monthly.
feel: **Anxious** but steadier than with two years.
S3.quote: Five years is enough to stop being the person who writes about pet food and become the person who gets it onto the shelf.
fieldNote: She uses AI to **hold her place** while she moves toward hands-on work.
She knows she may need **another change** at 35.
Paying down the **mortgage** is her main safety plan.

steps.text: Use AI tools for all online product descriptions
Ask to move into the field sales team within a year
Overpay the mortgage by about three hundred a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Okay, that I can plan around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming, but there's a decade, so let's be practical. I'd say it pretty calmly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, with ten years, the smartest thing I can do is pay off my flat before anyone needs to pay me for thinking. My job will change, maybe go, but if I own my home outright I can take a lower-paid job without fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd overpay the mortgage hard, around four hundred a month, so it's gone by about 2035. I'd stay in marketing a few more years and move to field sales or account work once I'm better with the numbers. Keep using the tools as they get better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Things are moving, but I can see my way through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is that realistic, paying it off in ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With what my nan left and the overpayments, roughly. I've done the sums twice. It means no fancy holidays, which I can live with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you change that plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If prices shot up or I lost my job early. Then I'd stop overpaying and just hold on to savings.

say: I'd say it's coming but a decade means being **practical**.
I'd say it **calmly** to friends and colleagues, without drama.
think: I think paying off **my flat** first is the smartest move.
I'd accept a **lower-paid** job without fear once I own my home.
do: Overpay the mortgage by about **four hundred** to clear it by 2035.
Move into **field sales** or account work once better with numbers.
feel: **Uneasy**, but I can see my way through.
S4.quote: With ten years, the smartest thing I can do is pay off my flat before anyone needs to pay me for thinking.
fieldNote: Her plan is about **owning her home**, not saving her current job.
She's **uneasy**, not anxious, because a paid-off flat makes job loss bearable.
She has a **fallback**: stop overpaying and hold savings if things go early.

steps.text: Overpay the mortgage about four hundred a month until 2035
Move into field sales or account work within a few years
Keep using new AI tools as they improve

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because of the mortgage and how fast it is. What would help is clear warning from my employer and some help with mortgage payments if a whole industry goes at once. I'm not a big believer or a big doubter, I just want to know which year to worry about.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about homes. People my age who own a flat and people who rent are going to feel these pictures very differently.

headlineQuote: I'm not a big believer or a big doubter, I just want to know which year to worry about.
portrait: Zoe is a 27-year-old **marketing assistant** at a pet food brand who writes product descriptions.
She owns a small flat thanks to an **inheritance**, with a mortgage and seven months saved.
She uses AI **now and then** and adopts it fully once it's proven.
In faster pictures she moves toward **field sales**, the hands-on side of getting food onto shelves.
Her steadiest plan is to **pay off her flat** before her desk work disappears.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because of how fast it comes with a **mortgage** to pay.
whatWouldHelp: **Clear warning** from her employer and **mortgage help** if a whole industry goes.
